note: British spelling (metre/dramatising/generalise/skilful) against the American-spelling rule.
replacement: There is another art that imitates by language alone, whether in prose or in verse. If it is in verse, it may mix different meters or keep to a single kind. This art has so far had no name. We have no common term for the mimes of Sophron and Xenarchus and the Socratic dialogues on the one hand, and for poetic imitations in iambic, elegiac, or any similar meter on the other. People do add the word 'maker' or 'poet' to the name of the meter, and speak of elegiac poets, or of epic (that is, hexameter) poets. They talk as if the imitation did not make the poet, and as if the verse alone entitled all of them, without distinction, to the name. Even when someone publishes a treatise on medicine or natural science in verse, custom gives its author the name of poet. Yet Homer and Empedocles have nothing in common except the meter, so it would be right to call the one a poet, and the other a physicist rather than a poet. By the same principle, suppose a writer in his poetic imitation were to combine all meters, as Chaeremon did in his Centaur, which is a medley of meters of every kind. We should still bring him under the general term poet. So much, then, for these distinctions.

replacement: Again, some arts use all the means mentioned above, namely rhythm, tune, and meter. Such are Dithyrambic and Nomic poetry, and also Tragedy and Comedy. The difference between them is this: the first two use all these means together, while the latter two use now one means, now another.

note: British spelling (metre/dramatising/generalise/skilful) against the American-spelling rule.
replacement: Imitation, then, is one instinct of our nature. Next there is the instinct for 'harmony' and rhythm, meters being plainly sections of rhythm. Starting from this natural gift, people gradually developed their special aptitudes, until their rude improvisations gave birth to Poetry.

note: British spelling (metre/dramatising/generalise/skilful) against the American-spelling rule.
replacement: Poetry then diverged in two directions, according to the individual character of the writers. The graver spirits imitated noble actions, and the actions of good men. The more trivial sort imitated the actions of meaner persons, and at first composed satires, just as the graver kind composed hymns to the gods and praises of famous men. We cannot assign a poem of the satirical kind to any author earlier than Homer, though there were probably many such writers. From Homer onward, however, instances can be cited, such as his own Margites and other similar compositions. The appropriate meter was introduced here too. That is why the measure is still called the iambic or lampooning measure, since it was the one in which people lampooned one another. So the older poets were distinguished as writers of heroic verse or of lampooning verse.

note: British spelling (metre/dramatising/generalise/skilful) against the American-spelling rule.
replacement: In the serious style Homer stands out among poets, for he alone combined dramatic form with excellence of imitation. In the same way he was the first to lay down the main lines of Comedy, by dramatizing the ludicrous instead of writing personal satire. His Margites bears the same relation to Comedy that the Iliad and Odyssey bear to Tragedy. But when Tragedy and Comedy came to light, the two classes of poets still followed their natural bent. The lampooners became writers of Comedy, and Tragedians succeeded the Epic poets, since the drama was a larger and higher form of art.

note: British spelling (metre/dramatising/generalise/skilful) against the American-spelling rule.
replacement: The successive changes through which Tragedy passed, and the authors of those changes, are well known. Comedy, by contrast, has had no history, because at first it was not treated seriously. It was late before the Archon granted a comic chorus to a poet; until then the performers were volunteers. Comedy had already taken definite shape by the time comic poets, distinctively so called, are heard of. Who gave it masks or prologues, or increased the number of actors, and other similar details, remain unknown. The plot originally came from Sicily. Among Athenian writers Crates was the first to give up the 'iambic' or lampooning form and to generalize his themes and plots.

note: British spelling (metre/dramatising/generalise/skilful) against the American-spelling rule.
replacement: Epic poetry agrees with Tragedy in being an imitation in verse of characters of a higher type. They differ in that Epic poetry admits only one kind of meter and is narrative in form. They differ, again, in length. Tragedy endeavors, as far as possible, to keep within a single revolution of the sun, or to exceed that limit only slightly, whereas the Epic action has no limits of time. This, then, is a second point of difference, although at first Tragedy was allowed the same freedom as Epic poetry.

note: British spelling (metre/dramatising/generalise/skilful) against the American-spelling rule.
replacement: What has been said also makes it evident that the poet's function is not to relate what has happened but what may happen, meaning what is possible according to the law of probability or necessity. Poet and historian are not distinguished by writing verse or prose. Herodotus could be put into verse, and his work would be no less a species of history in meter than without it. The real difference is that the historian relates what has happened and the poet what may happen. For this reason poetry is more philosophical and a higher thing than history: poetry tends to express the universal, and history the particular. By the universal I mean the kinds of things that a person of a certain type will say or do on occasion, according to the law of probability or necessity. Poetry aims at this universality when it attaches names to its personages. The particular is, for example, what Alcibiades did or suffered. Comedy already makes this apparent. There the poet first constructs the plot on the lines of probability and then inserts characteristic names, unlike the lampooners, who write about particular individuals. Tragedians, however, still keep to real names. The reason is that what is possible is credible. We are not at once sure that what has not happened is possible, whereas what has happened is manifestly possible, for otherwise it would not have happened. Even so, in some tragedies only one or two of the names are well known and the others are made up. In others none is well known, as in Agathon's Antheus, where incidents and names are alike invented, and still the play pleases just as much. So we must not cling at all costs to the received legends that Tragedy usually takes as its subjects. It would be absurd to try, since even the known subjects are known only to a few, and yet they please everyone. It follows plainly that the poet or 'maker' should be a maker of plots rather than of verses. He is a poet because he imitates, and what he imitates are actions. Even if he happens to take an historical subject, he is still a poet. Nothing prevents some events that really happened from conforming to the law of the probable and possible, and because they have that quality he is their poet or maker.

note: Source 'should arise' strengthened to 'must grow out'.
replacement: A Complex action is one where the change of fortune comes with Reversal, or with Recognition, or with both. These should grow out of the internal structure of the plot, so that what follows is the necessary or probable result of what came before. It makes all the difference whether a given event is a case of propter hoc or post hoc.

note: British spelling (metre/dramatising/generalise/skilful) against the American-spelling rule.
replacement: Actions that can have this effect must take place between persons who are friends, enemies, or indifferent to one another. When an enemy kills an enemy, nothing in the act or in the intention excites pity, except in so far as the suffering itself is pitiful. The same goes for indifferent persons. The poet should look instead for situations where the tragic incident occurs between people who are near or dear to one another. Examples are a brother who kills, or intends to kill, a brother, a son his father, a mother her son, a son his mother, or any other deed of that kind. The poet may not, indeed, destroy the framework of the received legends. He cannot change the fact, for instance, that Orestes killed Clytemnestra and Alcmaeon killed Eriphyle. But he ought to show invention of his own and handle the traditional material with skill. Let us explain more clearly what we mean by skillful handling.
